<!-- custom-release-notes:start -->
# Fragment-gate hardening: fail-closed quality gate, NUL-safe cleanup transport, bounded check-title, dispatch guards

## What

Collated delivery for the fragment-gate follow-up family from the #3276/#3297
review lineage:

- **#3283** — the pending-fragment quality gate no longer passes when git
  cannot answer. Merge-base resolution failures, changed/added diff failures,
  spawned-git timeouts, unusable repository roots (empty or malformed `.git`
  markers), and base-branch probe failures now fail the required `quality`
  context with an infrastructure-labeled message instead of "gate
  inconclusive, passing" — and an added-diff failure is no longer reported as
  an author-facing fragment VIOLATION. The documented non-repository /
  no-base local pass is preserved through positive marker-absence and
  positive ref-absence checks (locale-independent: git stderr is never
  consulted). With a git discovery override set (GIT_DIR et al.) the gate fails closed on a cwd git cannot describe, where the previous gate passed — fail-closed by design. Known limit: a MALFORMED (as opposed to absent) loose base ref
  also yields the ref-absence exit code and takes that documented pass —
  pre-existing behavior identical to the previous gate. `FRAGMENT_CHECK_ENFORCE=0`
  still soft-warns, now explicitly including infrastructure failures, for local runs.
- **#3299** — the `cleanup-release-fragments` arm in
  `release-and-publish.yml` now derives its changed-path list NUL-end-to-end
  (`git status --porcelain=v1 -z` through a jq reducer into the classifier's
  `--paths-format jsonl --changed-file` framing) instead of the legacy
  newline-delimited pipe that C-quoted and split adversarial paths before the
  classifier could see them. The snapshot stays before the cleanup commit,
  and the temp file is trap-cleaned.
- **#3300** — the `check-title` job in `pr-standards.yml` declares
  `timeout-minutes: 10`, closing the last unbounded job in that workflow.
- **#3307** — both dispatched run blocks that interpolate the
  `pr_number` input into `gh api` paths now refuse non-decimal values before
  any call; a concurrency group cancels superseded `pull_request` runs only
  (merge-group and dispatch runs get run-unique groups and are never
  cancelled, keeping merge-queue checks safe); the non-integer
  `changed_files` guard from #3297 and the least-privilege top-level
  permissions posture are pinned by tests that previously did not exist.

## Why

A required check that maps "cannot determine" to "pass" silently approves
user-visible PRs without release notes whenever git hiccups in CI, and a
lossy list transport can flip a required fragment verdict on paths the
classifier never faithfully saw. Both are fail-open shapes in the gate that
owns the repo's release-notes mandate.

## Verification

`tests/unit/scripts/check-pending-fragment-git.test.ts` (10 tests: real-git
failure legs plus `_internals.spawnSync` seam legs for deterministic timeout
and per-call failure shapes), `fragment-gate-cleanup-transport-3299.test.ts`
(byte-faithful reducer over synthetic porcelain `-z` records including quote-,
newline-, rename- and copy-bearing paths, plus full-pipeline composition on a
real scratch repository), `pr-standards-dispatch-guard-3307.test.ts`
(executed extracted run blocks with a call-recording `gh` stub, both
surfaces), `workflow-hardening.test.ts` (check-title bound, verbatim
concurrency expressions, permissions pin), and
`fragment-gate-workflow-contract.test.ts` (non-integer `changed_files` pin;
cleanup-arm mapping tests kept green).
<!-- custom-release-notes:end -->

# Fix: Full-Auto allows eleven audited read-only swarm tools without a critic

## What changed

Full-Auto's deterministic classifier now allows `skill_list`, `skill_inspect`, `external_skill_list`, `external_skill_inspect`, `knowledge_receipt_status`, `retrieve_lane_output`, `lean_turbo_plan_lanes`, `plan_conflict_check`, `scope_validate`, `context_status` and `suggest_patch` at the safe tier. Each was audited by reading the tool module and the functions it calls: none mutates project source or scope authority, spawns a process or uses the network on its default path. Previously each call escalated to the critic, a child session with a fixed prompt of roughly 43k tokens.

The classifier ignores arguments, so two narrow side effects ride along. `plan_conflict_check` completes the one-shot migration of legacy `.swarm/scopes/binding-*.json` files (for the session's project root the Full-Auto permission hook already performs the same migration) and spawns bounded read-only `git` only when called with `use_cochange: true`. `context_status` may record the model-limit telemetry in `.swarm/learning-health.json` that the context-budget hook already writes for the session's project root. Both accept a `working_directory` override, as older members of this tier do, so those effects can also land on another project root.

Every other swarm tool keeps escalating. Four read-shaped tools are deliberately excluded because they write on their default read path: `lean_turbo_status` and `lean_turbo_runner_status` (every read can archive state and seed a projection), `export_pr_review_partial_results` and `convene_general_council`.

`isReadOnlyTool` is shared, so these eleven names are also allowed in every state where read-only tools already are: while a Full-Auto run is paused or terminated, while its state file is unreadable, while a task awaits completion, and in strict mode. The same set also feeds read-only subagent delegation: with a `tool_filter.overrides` entry that limits a role to these names (for example `[read, grep, suggest_patch]`), delegating to that role is now allowed without a critic outside strict mode. Default capability maps are unchanged for all 26 roles.

`suggest_patch` is no longer listed as write-like (it never writes), so the read-only and write-like sets are disjoint. When `oldContent` does not match a protected path (per the central protected-path policy, plus `.env.*` variants), its `context-mismatch` error no longer echoes the file's actual lines. The check runs on the path as written and on its resolved real path, each also lower-cased, so directory links, Windows 8.3 short names and case variants of the lower-case protected names (`.env`, `.git`, `.swarm`, `package.json` and the lower-case prefixes) are covered. The two mixed-case policy entries, `CHANGELOG.md` and `CODEOWNERS`, are matched only in their exact spelling, which is a limit of the central policy itself.

## Why

Closes #3461. Follow-up to the "Classify the other 92 escalating tools" row left open in #3447.
<!-- custom-release-notes:end -->

# Task-gate evidence now records which plan it was earned under

## What

Task-gate evidence (`.swarm/evidence/{taskId}.json`) written under a plan now
carries an optional `planId` / `planIdentityHash` stamp, and the tools that
refuse or repair evidence use it to tell "this evidence belongs to an earlier
plan" apart from "this evidence is missing".

- When `update_task_status` refuses completion because the exact review route
  receipt is missing and the evidence is stamped for a different plan than the
  current `.swarm/plan.json`, the refusal says so and points at
  `repair_gate_evidence` instead of the generic missing-receipt message.
- `check_gate_status` adds a `prior_campaign_evidence` note (the gate `status`
  is unchanged) when the stamp names a different plan. Plan identity is advisory: it changes
  refusal wording and diagnostics only and is not itself a completion blocker.
- `repair_gate_evidence` may rebuild evidence stamped for a different plan even
  though it is otherwise structurally valid, and stamps the rebuilt record with
  the current plan identity.
- A stamp is only minted on new evidence, evidence that carries no recorded
  gates, or a non-duplicate coder `accepted_mutation` (a campaign restart). Evidence that carries forward
  previously recorded gates keeps the identity it was earned under, so a
  supplementary write (for example a todo scan) cannot launder old gates into
  the current plan.

## Why

When a plan is replaced with a different `swarm` or `title`, evidence for a
task id that the new plan reuses was indistinguishable from the new plan's own
evidence, so refusals gave no signal that the gates on file were earned under a
different plan.

## Limits

- Plan identity is advisory. It changes diagnostics and the wording of one
  refusal (the exact review-route-receipt branch of `update_task_status`); it is
  not a completion predicate and does not by itself unblock any task.
- The restart restamp is a heuristic. A coder `accepted_mutation` under a new
  plan restamps the record, but the designer, docs, sme, explorer and critic_*
  verifier gates the reducer keeps were earned earlier and still count toward
  completion, exactly as before this change. Conversely, a task with no coder
  step (docs, sme or explorer only) keeps its earlier stamp, so the advisory can
  flag it even though its gates were earned under the current plan; running
  `repair_gate_evidence` there discards those gates.
- The identity is read from raw `plan.json`; a byte-order mark or a transient
  read failure makes the identity unknown, which disables the advisory rather
  than producing a false one.
- Tasks that were already wedged before upgrading have no stamp, so they are
  treated as unknown and are not recovered by this release.
- The identity covers `swarm` and `title` only; replacing a plan without
  changing either does not change the identity.

## Migration

No action required. Evidence written before this change has no stamp and is
treated as unknown, not as prior-plan evidence: its behaviour, including
`repair_gate_evidence` refusing structurally valid evidence, is unchanged.
<!-- custom-release-notes:end -->

## Shell write-guard: interpreter spelling detection, host-reported shell grammar, and scope-gated eval routing

### Detection (#3343)

Inline-code interpreters are now classified as `interpreter_eval` writes
across the spelling families that evaded detection before: versioned
binaries (`python3.11`, `ruby3.2`, `node22.0.0`), forward-slash path-qualified
invocations (`/usr/bin/python3`, `C:/Python311/python.exe`), and
`env`/`command`/`exec`-wrapped forms — including wrapper CHAINS
(`command env python -c …`), `env` flags whether argument-less (`-i`) or
arg-taking (`-u NAME`, `-C dir`, `-S "opts"`), and `VAR=VALUE` assignments.
Previously any of these spellings evaded detection entirely, so the eval ran
completely unguarded. Known edges (each filed as a collated follow-up item): a backslash
path-qualified interpreter (`C:\Python311\python.exe -c …`) under a
Windows-grammar host still evades the interpreter tables (item 3); GNU
`env -S "python -c …"` (the command line INSIDE the -S split-string) is
consumed as a flag argument and not re-split (item 4 — the options-usage
form `env -S "-i" python -c …` IS classified); process-modifier wrappers
outside the env/command/exec family (`timeout 5 python -c …`, `stdbuf`,
`setsid`, `xargs`, `ionice`, `chrt`) are not unwrapped by the spelling
normalizer (item 5 — a distinct wrapper-inventory surface, final-critic r7);
and a stdin-delivered interpreter program (`echo CODE | python`, `python -`)
carries no eval flag and is not classified (item 6 — the pipe form admits
while the heredoc twin fails closed only by the parse gate; a distinct
delivery-mechanism surface, final-critic r7). This change's claims are bound
to the SPELLING axis of #3343 (versioned/path-qualified/env-command-exec
wrapped inline-code flags, including GNU/BSD getopt spellings of those
wrappers' flags).
Non-eval invocations (`python3.11 -m pytest`, `--version`, script paths)
remain unclassified, preserving the #1901 `-m` carve-out.

### Host-reported shell grammar (#3346)

The OpenCode 2 host reports the shell a `shell`-tool command actually
executes through the plugin `shell.create.before` hook (resolved once per
host process via the host's ShellSelect: user-configured shell, else
`$SHELL`, else on Windows pwsh → powershell → Git Bash → cmd). The write
gate and `/swarm guardrail explain` now key cmd/PowerShell grammar
inheritance on that authoritative report: a Windows host whose `shell` tool
runs Git Bash no longer misreads POSIX commands as `cmd.exe` (the #3323
false-positive class), and a PowerShell-executing host is covered on any
platform. Before the first host report (the first `shell` invocation of a
host session), the platform-keyed interim from #3326 applies — never wider
than the previous behavior. The v1 host (whose terminal tool is `bash`) is
unchanged.

### Scope-gated eval routing (#3347, and #3323 item 3)

Inspectable inline evals (`python -c`, `node -e`, …) no longer blanket-block
every role. They now route through the same universal-deny, file-authority,
and declared-scope checks as any other write, with the eval's **tracked
working directory** (following `cd` in the compound command) as the target:

- read-only roles (explorer, sme, …) are rejected by the file-authority
  check naming the role;
- agents with a declared scope: an eval whose working directory is inside
  the scope is admitted (`cd src && python -c …` for a `src/`-scoped coder);
  outside it, rejected with the declared-scope error;
- scope-less write-capable roles (architect, reviewer) KEEP the fail-closed
  eval block — the config-zone eval guard and #3347's own eval-block pins
  stay green. Whether orchestrator roles should also be unlocked is the
  open maintainer decision recorded on #3347 (its AC4);
- opaque eval classes (PowerShell `-EncodedCommand`, nested script blocks,
  dynamic `&`/IEX invocation) and dynamic redirect targets (`> $VAR`,
  `> $(cmd)`) keep their hard blocks;
- every same-interpre

# Coders can remove an empty directory outside their declared scope

## What

The shell write-scope gate no longer blocks a bare `rmdir <dir>` just because
the directory is outside the coder's declared scope, as long as the directory
is inside the workspace.

- Admitted: `rmdir <dir>` with no options and exactly one literal, unquoted
  operand whose location, with every symlink or junction in its parent chain
  resolved, is strictly inside the session workspace, when the command runs
  under a POSIX shell (the `bash` tool, or the `shell` tool on a non-Windows
  host). The target must not exist yet or must be a real directory.
- The exemption applies only to a plain command line, judged on the
  command text after the gate's existing `eval` / `sh -c` unwrapping. That
  text may hold only letters, digits, spaces, newlines and the characters
  `_ . / - = & | ; < >`, and every command in it must be one of `rmdir`,
  `mkdir`, `echo`, `true`, `false` or `test`. None of these commands can
  change the shell's working directory, and without `$`, quotes,
  backslashes, backticks, parentheses, braces, brackets or `#` nothing in
  that text can expand, be evaluated, be quoted, define a function or start
  a comment, so `rmdir` runs in the directory the gate checks and removes
  exactly the operand the gate checks. `&&` / `||` / `;` lists, pipelines,
  redirections such as `2>/dev/null`, `FOO=1 rmdir x` prefixes and `if` and
  loop bodies are fine:
  `rmdir .scratch-a/tmp1`, `rmdir dir/`, `rmdir ./dir`, `rmdir a && rmdir b`,
  `mkdir x && rmdir x`, `rmdir a 2>/dev/null || true`,
  `rmdir a && echo done` and `FOO=1 rmdir a` keep the exemption, and each
  `rmdir` of a distinct operand is judged separately.
- Every other line gives every `rmdir` in it the ordinary declared-scope
  check. That includes any text with a character outside the set above:
  `rmdir "dir"`, `rmdir a && echo "done"`, `echo $HOME; rmdir a`,
  `[ -d src ] && rmdir a`, subshells and brace groups (`(rmdir a)`,
  `{ rmdir a; }`), `case`, `$(...)`, backticks, any `#` (`rmdir d#/x`
  removes the one directory `d#/x` in bash, and `rmdir a # note` loses the
  exemption too), and paths containing `~ + , : @ %`. An interior tab is
  refused outright as unsafe command text, and an interior carriage return
  is never exempt either. It also includes any other
  command in the line: `cd`, `pushd`, `popd`, function
  definitions, `source` and `.`, `trap`, `alias`,
  an upper-case `RMDIR`, and every other command
  (`ls d && rmdir d`, `cd build && rmdir tmp`). A line with a
  here-document normally loses the exemption too, because the gate reads
  the body and delimiter lines as commands that must also be on the list
  (a body on a plain line cannot expand anything). This closes code that
  bash evaluates at run time, such as the bash 5.3 current-shell
  substitutions `${ cd ..; }` and `${| cd ..; }`, including a quoted one
  that arithmetic (`$((x))`) or a `test -v` / `[ -v` subscript evaluates.
- Unchanged (still blocked as before): `rmdir -p`, any other option
  (`--ignore-fail-on-non-empty`, `--`), several operands, globs, brace
  expansion, variables or command substitution in the operand, targets
  outside the workspace, symlink escapes, the workspace root itself, every
  recursive form (`rm -rf`, `rmdir /s`, `rd /s`), a target that exists as a
  file or symlink, and any `rmdir` run by a Windows executor (a
  `powershell -Command` / `pwsh -c` / `cmd /c` wrapper, a PowerShell-shaped
  command, or the `shell` tool on Windows). In PowerShell `rmdir` is an
  alias of `Remove-Item`, which also deletes files.
- Never exempt (the ordinary declared-scope check applies):
  - a sequence that names the same operand more than once, for example
    `rmdir a; cd ../other && rmdir a` or `rmdir a; rmdir -p a`, because the
    gate cannot tell those writes apart;
  - an operand with a `..` path segment (`link/../x`), even on a plain
    line;
  - repository c
